topic: Geometry (Lines, Angles, Triangles, Circles & Coordinate Geometry)

items.title: Lines, Angles & Parallel-Line Pairs
items.body:
### Lines, angles and parallel-line pairs

**The idea in one sentence**
When one slanting line crosses two parallel lines, the eight angles it makes fall into just a few families, and inside each family the angles are either exactly equal or add up to 180 degrees.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: two allied (same-side interior) angles between parallel lines are (2x + 20) and (3x − 30); find them.
1. Same-side interior angles add to 180 degrees, so write (2x + 20) + (3x − 30) = 180.
2. Collect: 5x − 10 = 180.
3. Add 10: 5x = 190, so x = 38.
4. Put x back: 2(38) + 20 = 96 degrees and 3(38) − 30 = 84 degrees; check 96 + 84 = 180.

**Why are same-side interior angles supplementary, not equal?**
They sit on the same side of the crossing line and together they wrap along one straight edge between the parallels, so they must fill a straight angle of 180 degrees rather than match each other.

**Picture**
```
      \
 ------a\b------   line 1
        \
 ------c\d------   line 2    corresponding: a and c equal
          \                  alternate interior: b and c equal
                             same-side interior: b and d add to 180
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| transversal | the line that cuts across both parallels |
| corresponding | same corner at each crossing |
| alternate | opposite sides of the transversal |
| supplementary | two angles adding to 180 degrees |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Corresponding, alternate-interior and alternate-exterior angles are equal; same-side interior (allied) angles add to 180 degrees; a linear pair on a straight line adds to 180 degrees; vertically opposite angles are equal; angles around a single point add to 360 degrees.

**Exam-level example**
A transversal makes an angle of 65 degrees with the first parallel line; find the same-side interior angle at the second line. Equal pairs would give 65 degrees, but the same-side interior partner is supplementary, so it is 180 − 65 = 115 degrees. Check: 65 + 115 = 180, which is the straight angle the two share.

**Common traps**
- Treating same-side interior angles as equal when they are supplementary.
- Using the complement (90 minus the angle) instead of the supplement (180 minus the angle).
- Forgetting that only parallel lines guarantee these equalities.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| corresponding, alternate = equal | same angle on parallels |
| same-side interior = 180 | they add to a straight angle |
| vertically opposite = equal | the X-cross angles match |
| round a point = 360 | full turn |
keyPoints: Corresponding and alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.
Same-side interior (allied) angles are supplementary, adding to 180 degrees.
Complementary angles add to 90 degrees; linear pairs add to 180 degrees.
Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles around a point total 360 degrees.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Concept of Point and Line; Angles

items.title: Triangles — Angles, Pythagoras, Similarity
items.body:
### Triangles — angles, Pythagoras and similarity

**The idea in one sentence**
Every triangle obeys fixed angle and side rules, a right-angled one lets you find the slanting side by Pythagoras, and two same-shape triangles have sides in one ratio but areas in that ratio squared.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: a right triangle has the two shorter sides 9 cm and 12 cm; find the longest side.
1. In a right triangle the longest side (hypotenuse) faces the right angle.
2. Pythagoras says the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the other two squared: 9 × 9 + 12 × 12 = 81 + 144 = 225.
3. Take the square root: √225 = 15.
4. So the hypotenuse is 15 cm — this is just the 3-4-5 triangle enlarged three times.

**Why does area scale as the ratio squared, not the ratio itself?**
Area covers two directions at once; if every length is k times bigger, both directions stretch by k, so the area grows by k times k.

**Picture**
```
     |\
   9 | \  hypotenuse = sqrt(9^{2} + 12^{2}) = 15
     |__\
      12
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| hypotenuse | the longest side, opposite the right angle |
| k | the ratio of matching sides of two similar triangles |
| k² | k multiplied by itself, the area ratio |
| remote interior | the two inside angles away from an exterior angle |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Interior angles add to 180 degrees; an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles; each side lies strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two; for right triangles hypotenuse² = base² + height² (triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25); for similar triangles sides scale by k, perimeter by k, area by k².

**Exam-level example**
Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 3 to 5 and the smaller one has area 36 cm². The area ratio is (5 ÷ 3)² = 25 ÷ 9, so the larger area is 36 × 25 ÷ 9 = 100 cm². Check: taking the square root of the area ratio, √(100 ÷ 36) = 10 ÷ 6 = 5 ÷ 3, which matches the side ratio.

**Common traps**
- Applying the side ratio straight to areas instead of squaring it first.
- Using Pythagoras on a triangle that is not right-angled.
- Breaking the triangle inequality, for example calling 9, 12 and 21 a triangle when 9 + 12 is only 21.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| angles add to 180 | the triangle angle sum |
| hyp² = base² + height² | right-triangle side rule |
| sides × k, area × k² | similar-triangle scaling |
| diff < c < sum | the triangle inequality |
keyPoints: Interior angles add to 180 degrees; an exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles.
A side lies strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two.
Right triangles only: hypotenuse² = base² + height² (triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13).
Similar triangles: sides and perimeter scale by k, area by k².
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Basic concept of Triangle; Similarity & Congruency

items.title: Triangle Centres & the Angle Bisector Theorem
items.body:
### Triangle centres and the angle bisector theorem

**The idea in one sentence**
Three special lines of a triangle each meet at one point, giving four named centres, and the bisector of a corner splits the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides beside it.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: in triangle ABC the bisector from A meets BC at D; AB = 6, AC = 8, BC = 14; find BD.
1. The bisector theorem says BD to DC equals AB to AC, which is 6 to 8, simplified to 3 to 4.
2. The whole base BC of 14 is split into 3 + 4 = 7 equal parts.
3. One part is 14 ÷ 7 = 2.
4. BD takes 3 parts: 3 × 2 = 6, and DC takes 4 parts: 4 × 2 = 8; check 6 + 8 = 14.

**Why does the centroid sit two-thirds of the way from the vertex?**
The centroid is the balance point of the triangle; it must sit closer to the heavier spread of area away from a vertex, and geometry fixes that split at exactly 2 parts from the vertex to 1 part to the opposite side.

**Picture**
```
        A
       /|\
      / G \     G = centroid, AG : G-to-midpoint = 2 : 1
     /__|__\
    B   D   C    AD is a median; bisector gives BD:DC = AB:AC
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Centre | How it is built |
|---|---|
| centroid | the three medians meet |
| incentre | the three angle bisectors meet |
| circumcentre | the three side perpendicular-bisectors meet |
| orthocentre | the three altitudes meet |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
The centroid divides each median 2 to 1 from the vertex; the incentre is equidistant from the sides and holds the inscribed circle; the circumcentre is equidistant from the vertices (and in a right triangle sits at the midpoint of the hypotenuse); the orthocentre is where the altitudes meet (the right-angle vertex in a right triangle); the bisector from A gives BD to DC equal to AB to AC.

**Exam-level example**
A median of a triangle is 18 cm long; how far is the vertex from the centroid? The centroid takes the 2-part of the 2-to-1 split, so the vertex-to-centroid distance is (2 ÷ 3) × 18 = 12 cm, leaving 6 cm to the opposite side. Check: 12 + 6 = 18, and 12 to 6 is indeed 2 to 1.

**Common traps**
- Measuring the 2-to-1 centroid split from the wrong end (the 2-part is from the vertex).
- Placing the circumcentre inside every triangle; in an obtuse triangle it lies outside.
- Confusing the incentre (bisectors) with the circumcentre (perpendicular bisectors).

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| centroid 2:1 | from vertex, bigger part first |
| circumcentre = hyp midpoint | in a right triangle |
| BD:DC = AB:AC | angle bisector split |
| incentre inside always | holds the inscribed circle |
keyPoints: The centroid divides each median 2 to 1 measured from the vertex.
A right triangle's circumcentre is the hypotenuse midpoint; its orthocentre is the right-angle vertex.
The incentre is where the angle bisectors meet and is always inside.
Angle bisector theorem: the bisector from A gives BD to DC equal to AB to AC.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Centroid; Circumcentre; Angle Bisector

items.title: Circles & Polygon Angles
items.body:
### Circles and polygon angles

**The idea in one sentence**
Angles made by a circle follow a doubling rule between the centre and the edge, and the angles of any many-sided figure are fixed by its number of sides.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: a regular polygon has each exterior angle 24 degrees; how many sides, and what is the interior-angle sum?
1. As you walk once around any polygon you turn through a full 360 degrees in total.
2. Each corner turns you by one exterior angle, here 24 degrees, so the number of corners is 360 ÷ 24 = 15.
3. So the polygon has 15 sides.
4. Interior-angle sum is (number of sides − 2) × 180 = (15 − 2) × 180 = 13 × 180 = 2340 degrees.

**Why is the central angle twice the inscribed angle?**
Both stand on the same arc, but the centre sees the arc from inside while an edge point sees it from farther back; the geometry of the isosceles radii shows the inside view is always exactly double the edge view.

**Picture**
```
        O (centre)         central angle at O = 2 x inscribed angle
       / \                 angle in a semicircle = 90 degrees
      /   \
   A .--arc--. B
       \   /
        \ /
         P (on circle)   inscribed angle at P
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| inscribed angle | an angle with its corner on the circle |
| central angle | an angle with its corner at the centre |
| tangent | a line touching the circle at one point |
| n | the number of sides of a polygon |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Central angle is twice any inscribed angle on the same arc; the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees; a tangent meets the radius at a right angle so the tangent length from a point at distance d is √(d² − r²); an n-gon has interior-angle sum (n − 2) × 180 and exterior-angle sum 360.

**Exam-level example**
From a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, find the tangent length. The tangent and radius meet at a right angle, so the tangent is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Check: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13², the right-triangle relation.

**Common traps**
- Taking the central angle as equal to, rather than double, the inscribed angle.
- Forgetting the exterior angles always total 360 degrees whatever the number of sides.
- Using the full distance d as the tangent length instead of √(d² − r²).

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| central = 2 × inscribed | same-arc doubling rule |
| semicircle angle = 90 | angle on a diameter |
| tangent = √(d² − r²) | length from an outside point |
| (n−2) × 180 | interior-angle sum |
keyPoints: Central angle is twice any inscribed angle on the same arc; a semicircle angle is 90 degrees.
A tangent meets the radius at a right angle; tangent length is √(d² − r²).
An n-gon has interior-angle sum (n − 2) × 180 degrees.
Every polygon's exterior angles total 360 degrees; a regular one has each exterior 360 ÷ n.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Basic concept of Circle; Theorems of circle; Angles

items.title: Coordinate Geometry — Distance, Section, Slope & Area
items.body:
### Coordinate geometry — distance, section, slope and area

**The idea in one sentence**
Once points are given as number pairs, every length, dividing point, steepness and enclosed area can be read straight off the coordinates with a small set of formulas.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: find the distance between A(2, 3) and B(7, 15).
1. Find how far apart they are left-to-right: 7 − 2 = 5.
2. Find how far apart they are up-and-down: 15 − 3 = 12.
3. These two gaps make a right angle, so the straight distance is the hypotenuse: √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169.
4. √169 = 13, so the distance is 13 units.

**Why does the section formula weight the far point by the near ratio?**
To land a point one-third of the way from A to B you must lean mostly on A, so the formula multiplies each endpoint by the opposite share; the ratio numbers cross over, which is the detail most learners slip on.

**Picture**
```
  B(7,15)
     |\
  12 | \  distance = sqrt(5^{2} + 12^{2}) = 13
     |__\
  A(2,3) 5
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Δx, Δy | the left-right and up-down gaps between two points |
| slope | how steep a line is, up-down gap over left-right gap |
| m : n | the ratio in which a point splits a segment |
| collinear | three points lying on one straight line |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Distance is √(Δx² + Δy²); the midpoint is the average of the two x values and of the two y values; the internal section point for ratio m to n is ((m·x₂ + n·x₁) ÷ (m + n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁) ÷ (m + n)); slope is Δy ÷ Δx; parallel lines share a slope and perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to −1; the triangle area is half the absolute value of x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂), and a zero area means the three points are collinear.

**Exam-level example**
Divide A(2, 3) and B(8, 15) internally in the ratio 1 to 2. x = (1 × 8 + 2 × 2) ÷ 3 = 12 ÷ 3 = 4; y = (1 × 15 + 2 × 3) ÷ 3 = 21 ÷ 3 = 7, giving (4, 7). Check: the point is one-third of the way from A, nearer A as the ratio 1 to 2 demands.

**Common traps**
- Crossing the ratio weights the wrong way in the section formula.
- Taking only Δy as the distance and forgetting Δx.
- Expecting equal slopes for perpendicular lines when their slopes multiply to −1.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| √(Δx² + Δy²) | distance between two points |
| average the coordinates | the midpoint |
| Δy ÷ Δx | the slope |
| area 0 | the three points are collinear |
keyPoints: Distance is √(Δx² + Δy²); the midpoint is the average of the coordinates.
Internal section point for m to n: ((m·x₂ + n·x₁) ÷ (m + n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁) ÷ (m + n)).
Slope is Δy ÷ Δx; parallel lines share slopes, perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
Triangle area uses the coordinate formula; a zero area means the points are collinear.

items.title: Tangent pairs, tangential quadrilaterals & integer-triangle counting
items.body:
### Tangent pairs, tangential quadrilaterals and counting integer triangles

**The idea in one sentence**
Two tangents from one outside point are equal and set up a neat right-angle quadrilateral, a four-sided figure with an inscribed circle has equal sums of opposite sides, and counting whole-number triangles for a fixed perimeter is a short, careful list.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: how many triangles with whole-number sides have perimeter 14?
1. Write sides smallest to largest, a ≤ b ≤ c, adding to 14, with a + b greater than c.
2. Because a + b is greater than c and all three add to 14, c must be below 7, so c is at most 6.
3. For c = 6: (2,6,6), (3,5,6), (4,4,6) — three triangles.
4. For c = 5: (4,5,5) — one more. Total four. Note (2,5,7) fails because 2 + 5 is not greater than 7.

**Why must the largest side be below half the perimeter?**
If the largest side reached half the perimeter, the other two together would only equal it, making a flat line, not a triangle; staying below half keeps the two shorter sides long enough to close up.

**Picture**
```
        A ______ B
        /        \     tangents PA, PB from P are equal
    P .<   O (centre)   angle P + angle O = 180
        \________/      tangential quad: AB + CD = BC + AD
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| P | the external point the tangents come from |
| O | the centre of the circle |
| tangential quadrilateral | a four-sided figure with a circle touching all sides |
| P (perimeter) | the total of all sides |

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Two tangents from a point are equal and the angle between them plus the central angle equals 180 degrees; in a tangential quadrilateral the sums of opposite sides are equal, AB + CD = BC + AD; to count whole-number triangles of perimeter P, list a ≤ b ≤ c adding to P with a + b greater than c, where the largest side c stays below P ÷ 2.

**Exam-level example**
A circle touches all four sides of quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 8, BC = 9, CD = 7; find AD. Equal sums of opposite sides give AB + CD = BC + AD, so 8 + 7 = 9 + AD, which means 15 = 9 + AD and AD = 6 cm. Check: 8 + 7 = 15 and 9 + 6 = 15, the two sums match.

**Common traps**
- Forgetting to keep a ≤ b ≤ c, which double-counts the same triangle.
- Including a flat set such as (2,5,7) where the two shorter sides only equal the longest.
- Mixing up the tangent angle with the central angle, which are supplementary, not equal.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| two tangents equal | same length from one point |
| angle P + angle O = 180 | tangent and central angle |
| AB + CD = BC + AD | tangential quadrilateral |
| c below P ÷ 2 | largest side limit when counting |
keyPoints: Two tangents from a point are equal; the tangent angle plus the central angle is 180 degrees.
Tangential quadrilateral: AB + CD = BC + AD (equal sums of opposite sides).
Count integer triangles by listing a ≤ b ≤ c adding to P with a + b greater than c.
The largest side stays below P ÷ 2; perimeter 14 and perimeter 11 each give 4 triangles.
items.mnemonic: Tangents: ∠P + ∠O = 180°. Tangential quad: opposite sides sum equal. Counting: c < P/2 and a+b>c.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Theorems of circle; Triangle inequality
